overview: This file documents the transition from wartime intelligence gathering on Japanese industry to U.S. planning and assessment for the occupation of Japan in 1945. It includes reports on industrial locations, wartime production, corporate influence, and munitions reorganization; a substantial secret policy paper considering how to demilitarize heavy industry while preserving civilian subsistence, economic recovery, and reparations; discussion of Japan’s dependence on imports and export markets; and SCAP’s first detailed inventories of surviving industrial capacity in textiles, shipbuilding, telecommunications, nonferrous metals, electric power, iron and steel, coal, and petroleum. Together, the documents reveal how American officials evaluated Japan’s industrial system both as the foundation of its former military power and as a necessary basis for postwar reconstruction and foreign trade.
interest: The file is especially valuable because it captures policy formation at the precise moment when Japan changed from an enemy war economy into an occupied country whose civilian survival and recovery depended upon retaining some industrial capacity. The lengthy heavy-industry paper exposes tensions among demilitarization, reparations, minimum living standards, and economic revival, while the December inventories provide an unusually broad statistical baseline of surviving plant, output potential, war damage, and material and labor shortages. Its coverage of facilities and resources across Japan’s former empire also helps historians trace how imperial economic networks were dismantled and how the loss of overseas supplies shaped postwar planning.
